documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
70-year-old man moving his primary care to us; his previous internist cut back hours and he wanted easier access. Retired after a long career teaching high school math. Sees an outside cardiology group yearly since a stent to the right coronary artery in early 2022. Feels well today. No chest pressure, no dyspnea on his usual 2-mile walks, no palpitations, no lightheadedness. Knees ache after long walks or yardwork, worse going downstairs; takes acetaminophen a few times a week, never needed injections.

PMH: HTN, type 2 DM (on metformin for roughly a decade, never on insulin), hyperlipidemia, CAD s/p DES to RCA 2022, OA both knees.
PSH: R inguinal hernia repair 2000; DES to RCA 2022; L cataract extraction with lens implant early 2023.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, acetaminophen 500 mg prn.
Allergies: penicillin (hives as a young adult); shellfish (mild hives).
Family: father had a heart attack at 72. Mother had high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes. Older brother has coronary disease.
Social: former smoker, about 30 pack-years, stopped in 2016. Wine on weekends, a glass or two. Lives in Amherst, still tutors a few students in algebra.

Exam: vitals as charted. Alert, comfortable. Lenses: left implant, right clear. Neck supple, no carotid bruits. Heart regular, normal S1 S2, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, healed right groin scar. Knees with bony enlargement and mild crepitus bilaterally, no effusion, full extension. Feet: intact monofilament and vibration, pulses 2+, skin intact.

A/P
1. HTN: at goal on lisinopril 20. BMP today.
2. T2DM: CMP, A1c, urine microalbumin today. Eye exam due this fall, he has an ophthalmologist.
3. Hyperlipidemia / CAD with stent: continue atorvastatin 40 and aspirin. Lipids today. Keep his cardiology follow-up.
4. Knee OA: acetaminophen is fine, avoid regular NSAIDs given ASA and kidneys.
5. Former heavy smoker within 15 years of quitting: eligible for yearly low-dose CT, ordered. One-time aorta ultrasound ordered.
6. HCV screen today. Vaccines: high-dose flu, updated COVID and PCV20 at a nurse visit in October; shingles series after that.
7. Records request sent to the prior office.
Follow up in about 6 months, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Your recent labs

- Drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery, February 2022, outside cardiology; cath summary included.
- Left cataract extraction with lens implant, March 2023, outside ophthalmology.
- Tdap October 2018. No pneumococcal vaccine on record.
- Meds and allergies match ours.
Original paper to scanning. Flagged for PCP review.

Initial wellness visit. Health risk assessment reviewed with him.
Function: independent in all daily activities, drives, manages his own pills with a weekly box. Hearing fine in conversation. No falls this year. Sleeps 7 hours.
Mood: PHQ-2 is 0.
Cognition: clock drawing and 3-word recall normal.
Habits: walks most mornings, gardens; wine on weekends only; no tobacco since 2016.
Screening status: colonoscopy 2019 normal, no repeat planned. Lung CT last October negative, due again this fall. Aorta ultrasound normal. HCV done. Vaccines: flu/COVID/PCV20 last fall, Shingrix complete, Tdap 2018.
Advance directive: has a health care proxy on file with his lawyer, will bring a copy.
Exam: vitals as charted. Regular rhythm, no murmur. Lungs clear. Feet: sensation intact to monofilament, pulses 2+, no calluses or ulcers.

documents.title: Lightheaded spells
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Called me back after a message to the nurse line. For the past several days he gets a wave of lightheadedness, feels he might pass out, mostly when he gets up fast from a chair and a couple of times partway through his morning walk. Sits down and it passes in under a minute. Never lost consciousness, no fall, no chest pain or pressure, no palpitations he can name. Eating and drinking normally, no vomiting or diarrhea, no black stools, no new drugs. Home cuff last night 126/72, the machine read his pulse as 51, which is lower than he's used to.
With his coronary history and a slow pulse, I'd like his cardiologist to see him this week rather than me first. Called his cardiology group; they can see him Wednesday the 25th. Told him: no driving if he feels any of this coming on, sit or lie down with symptoms, call 911 for chest pain, fainting or if it gets worse. He understands and agrees.

conditions.label: Atrioventricular block, second degree
conditions.note: Type I (progressive PR prolongation with dropped beats)

reports.text: Ventricular rate about 50. Sinus P waves at a regular rate, conducted with a PR interval that lengthens beat to beat until one P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle restarts, giving grouped beating. QRS narrow. Normal axis. No acute ST-segment change.
reports.conclusion: Sinus rhythm with second-degree AV block, type I. No acute ischemic change.

documents.title: Cardiology office visit
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group. Date of service 09/25/2024.
RE: Raymond Becker, 71. Copy to primary care.

Known to our practice since his right coronary stent in 2022. His PCP asked us to see him promptly. Over roughly the past week he has had a handful of spells where he feels he is going to black out, mostly on standing quickly and at times while walking. No actual syncope. No chest discomfort, no exertional dyspnea.

Current medicines: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, acetaminophen as needed. He takes no beta-blocker, calcium channel blocker or digoxin.
Allergies: penicillin (hives), shellfish (mild hives).

BP 130/70, pulse 50 and irregularly regular. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.

ECG today: sinus rhythm with progressive PR lengthening and a non-conducted P wave, grouped beating; narrow QRS; no acute ST change.

Impression: second-degree AV block, type I. This is usually block within the AV node and often benign, but he is symptomatic, so we want to see how much block he has across day and night and whether his spells line up with it.

Plan:
- 14-day ambulatory ECG patch, applied in the office Friday.
- He takes no AV-nodal slowing drugs, nothing to stop. Avoid adding any.
- Rise slowly, sit at the first sign of a spell; call or go to the ED for any faint.
- We will review the monitor with him and write again.

reports.text: Extended ambulatory ECG recording, 14 days (09/27/2024 to 10/11/2024), analyzable time 99%. Predominant rhythm sinus. Heart rate minimum 41 (asleep), average 58, maximum 104. Intermittent second-degree AV block, type I, throughout the recording, more frequent at night. Longest pause 2.4 seconds, during sleep, from a non-conducted P wave. No type II second-degree block. No complete heart block. No atrial fibrillation or flutter. Rare isolated premature ventricular beats. Two patient-triggered events (lightheaded) correspond to type I block episodes.
reports.conclusion: Intermittent second-degree AV block, type I, with symptom correlation. No higher-grade block. Longest pause 2.4 seconds.

documents.title: Cardiology letter: monitor results
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group. Telephone review with the patient 10/17/2024.

The two-week patch shows intermittent type I second-degree AV block, mostly at night, with an average rate of 58 and a longest pause of 2.4 seconds. There is no type II block, no complete block and no atrial arrhythmia. His two lightheaded entries occurred during block episodes.

Since the visit he has been getting up more slowly and the spells are much less frequent; none in the last several days. With nodal-level block, no higher-grade block and improving symptoms, a pacemaker is not indicated at this time.

Plan: observe. Avoid beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and other AV-nodal agents. Return promptly for syncope or worsening symptoms. Yearly visit here with an ECG. Current medicines unchanged.

conditions.label: ST elevation (STEMI) myocardial infarction involving right coronary artery

reports.text: Ventricular rate 42. Sinus P waves with grouped QRS complexes; PR interval lengthens until a P wave fails to conduct. ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Narrow QRS.
reports.conclusion: Acute inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Second-degree AV block, type I.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department. Arrived 04/03/2026 06:20 by ambulance.

72-year-old man with coronary disease (right coronary stent 2022) and a known type I second-degree AV block. Woke around 05:30 with abrupt crushing pain behind the breastbone running into the left arm and up into the jaw. Sweaty and a little nauseated on arrival. No vomiting, no syncope.

Home medicines: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, acetaminophen as needed.
Allergies: penicillin (hives); shellfish (hives).

Triage: BP 92/60, HR 42, SpO2 97% on room air. Pale, diaphoretic. Slow irregular pulse. Lungs clear. No JVD. No murmur.

ECG 06:26: ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Telemetry shows grouped beats with lengthening PR intervals and periodic dropped QRS complexes.

Course: STEMI alert called 06:28. Aspirin 324 mg chewed, clopidogrel 600 mg orally, heparin bolus per protocol. Atropine 0.5 mg IV once for the slow rate and low pressure; HR came up to 58 and BP to 104/66. Pads placed, not used. Initial high-sensitivity troponin I 62 ng/L. To the cath lab at 07:20.

Impression: acute inferior STEMI; second-degree AV block, type I.
Disposition: cath lab, then cardiac unit.

medications.sig: Place 1 tablet under the tongue every 5 minutes as needed for chest pain, up to 3 doses; call 911 if pain persists

reports.text: Emergent coronary angiography and PCI. Access: right radial artery, 6 French. Left main normal. Left anterior descending: mild nonobstructive disease. Circumflex: mild nonobstructive disease. Right coronary artery: acute thrombotic total occlusion of the proximal vessel, above the previously placed stent; the prior stent itself patent beyond. Thrombus aspiration not performed. Predilation, then one drug-eluting stent deployed in the proximal RCA with good expansion. Final TIMI 3 flow, no residual stenosis, no dissection. Heart rate 50s to 60s throughout without pacing. Radial band applied.
reports.conclusion: Acute proximal RCA occlusion treated with one drug-eluting stent, TIMI 3 flow. Mild nonobstructive LAD and circumflex disease.

reports.text: Left ventricle normal in size with normal wall thickness. Hypokinesis of the inferior wall. Other segments contract normally. LVEF 50% by biplane method. Right ventricle normal in size and function. Atria normal in size. No significant valve disease. No pericardial effusion. Inferior vena cava normal with normal collapse.
reports.conclusion: LVEF 50% with inferior wall hypokinesis. No significant valve disease. No effusion.

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Regional hospital, cardiology service. Admitted 04/03/2026, discharged 04/06/2026.
Diagnoses: acute inferior ST-elevation MI, proximal right coronary artery; coronary artery disease with prior RCA stent (2022); second-degree AV block, type I; hypertension; type 2 diabetes; hyperlipidemia.
Allergies: penicillin (hives); shellfish (hives).

Course: Presented through our ED with an inferior STEMI and slow type I block (HR 42, BP 92/60), which responded to a single dose of atropine. Emergent angiography by the right radial route found an acute thrombotic occlusion of the proximal RCA above his old stent; treated with one drug-eluting stent, TIMI 3 flow. LAD and circumflex had only mild disease. High-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 21,350 ng/L. Echo 4/4: LVEF 50%, inferior hypokinesis, no significant valve disease. On telemetry after reperfusion he returned to his baseline sinus rhythm with intermittent type I block, rates 52 to 64; no temporary pacing was needed. Lisinopril was held the first day for soft pressures and restarted 4/5. Metformin held 48 hours after contrast; creatinine stayed normal, restarted at discharge. No beta-blocker given the AV block and resting rate. Pain free from the cath lab onward, walking the halls without symptoms.

Discharge medicines:
- aspirin 81 mg daily (continue indefinitely)
- clopidogrel 75 mg daily (NEW; 12 months, do not stop without cardiology)
- atorvastatin 80 mg daily (INCREASED from 40 mg)
- lisinopril 20 mg daily
- metformin 1000 mg twice daily (resume 4/6)
- nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL as needed for chest pain (NEW)
- acetaminophen 500 mg as needed

Follow-up: primary care within 7 to 14 days; cardiology clinic in 5 to 6 weeks; referral placed for phase II cardiac rehabilitation. No driving for 1 week, no lifting over 10 lb with the right arm for 48 hours. Radial site clean at discharge.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Transitional care call, discharge summary received this morning. Home since Monday afternoon. No chest pain, no need for nitro. Tired but up and about. Wrist site a small bruise, no swelling or bleeding. Picked up clopidogrel, atorvastatin 80 and the nitro tablets; we went through his list and he has stopped the 40 mg atorvastatin. Rehab has not called yet, gave him the number to follow up. Appointment with PCP 4/14 confirmed. Reviewed when to call 911.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 11 days after an inferior STEMI with a new drug-eluting stent in the proximal RCA (hospital 4/3 to 4/6; discharge summary and ED record reviewed). He's glad he called the ambulance instead of waiting. Since home: no chest pain, no nitro used, no lightheadedness. More tired than usual, napping in the afternoon. Walking 10 minutes twice a day. Rehab intake is 4/28.
Meds reconciled against the discharge list: aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75 (new), atorvastatin 80 (up from 40), lisinopril 20, metformin 1000 BID, SL nitro prn, acetaminophen prn. No bleeding or bruising beyond the wrist, no muscle aches on the higher statin.
Exam: vitals as charted. R radial site healed, pulse 2+. Heart: slow grouped rhythm, no murmur or rub. Lungs clear. No edema.
A/P
1. Inferior STEMI s/p RCA DES: doing well. DAPT for 12 months, reinforced not to stop clopidogrel for any procedure without asking cardiology. Nitro instructions reviewed. Cardiac rehab start 4/28. Cardiology visit mid-May.
2. AV block type I: unchanged, no beta-blocker per cardiology.
3. HTN: pressure fine on lisinopril. BMP today after contrast and ACE restart.
4. T2DM: metformin back on. A1c at the June visit.
5. Lipids on atorvastatin 80: recheck in June.
See me in about 2 months.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, ventricular rate 56, with intermittent progressive PR prolongation and non-conducted P waves. Q waves in II, III and aVF. ST segments returned to baseline. Narrow QRS.
reports.conclusion: Second-degree AV block, type I. Inferior Q waves consistent with recent inferior infarction.

documents.title: Cardiology follow-up letter
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology group. Date of service 05/13/2026. Copy to primary care.

Six weeks after an inferior STEMI treated with a proximal RCA drug-eluting stent. No angina, no nitroglycerin use, no dizziness or near-fainting. Began phase II cardiac rehabilitation 4/28 and is going three mornings a week. Energy improving.

Medicines: aspirin 81 mg, clopidogrel 75 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, SL nitroglycerin as needed, acetaminophen as needed.
Allergies: penicillin, shellfish.

BP 122/72, HR 56. Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema. Radial site healed.
ECG: type I second-degree AV block with inferior Q waves; ST segments back to baseline.

Assessment and plan:
- Recent inferior MI, recovering well. Continue DAPT through April 2027, then aspirin alone.
- Atorvastatin 80 mg; please recheck a lipid panel at his next primary care visit.
- Type I AV block, baseline; no beta-blocker. Continue to avoid AV-nodal agents.
- Complete cardiac rehab. Return here in 6 months.
